lead: An op-amp is not one circuit. It is a chain of four jobs: read the difference between two inputs, multiply it by a very large number, move the DC level to where the output stage needs it, and drive current into a load. Each job is a separate stage. The stages share bias currents and are designed together. This chain explains why an op-amp has high input resistance, huge open-loop gain, and low output resistance. The 741 is the classic example.
prereq: You need: 5.1 and 5.4; Unit 4 negative feedback for closed-loop later.

blocks.text: The input stage is a differential pair. Two matched transistors, Q1 and Q2, share a tail current source. The input voltage difference v_id steers the tail current: one side takes more, the other less. An active-load current mirror turns this balanced change into a single-ended current at the next stage. The stage sets three important op-amp properties. Its bias current sets input resistance and input bias current. Mismatch between Q1 and Q2 and the load mirror sets input offset voltage. The tail source output resistance and the mirror matching set common-mode rejection ratio, CMRR. For a MOSFET pair the gate draws almost no DC current, so input resistance is set by the bias network; for a BJT pair base current sets it. The input stage also gives gain, Av1, but not the whole open-loop gain. In the 741 the first stage is this kind of differential pair with an active load. See 5.1 and 5.4.

The gain stage gives most of the voltage gain. It is a common-emitter (CE) stage with a BJT, or a common-source (CS) stage with a MOSFET, loaded by a current source or current mirror. A high load resistance at the output node turns a small current change into a large voltage change. That is why Av2 in the worked example is 500, much larger than Av1. The same high-resistance node is where Miller compensation is placed: a capacitor from the gain-stage output back to its input, covered in 5.7.

The level shifter sits between the gain stage and the output stage. The gain-stage output has a DC level that is too high for the output stage input. The level shifter moves that DC level down without changing the signal much. Common forms are an emitter follower or source follower with a current source, or a resistor divider. Its signal gain is near 1, not a new gain stage; in the example Av3 = 0.5 shows it can even attenuate. It must present a light load to the gain stage, or it will reduce Av2. Some syllabi call the gain stage the intermediate stage and the output stage the output buffer.

The output stage is a class AB push-pull buffer. An NPN and a PNP transistor (or an NMOS and a PMOS) source or sink load current. Small bias diodes or a bias network keep both devices slightly on, so crossover distortion is low. The stage has voltage gain near 1, Av4 = 0.98 in the example, but it has current gain. That current gain gives low output resistance and the ability to drive a load such as a speaker, cable, or ADC input. A short-circuit limit protects the output devices when the load current is too high. The output swing is not the full supply: saturation voltages and device drops stop it short of the rails. The overall open-loop gain is the product of the four stage gains.
A_ol = Av1 × Av2 × Av3 × Av4, and A_dB = 20 log₁₀ |A_ol|
blocks.where: A_ol is the open-loop voltage gain in V/V; Av1 is the input-stage voltage gain; Av2 is the gain-stage voltage gain; Av3 is the level-shifter voltage gain; Av4 is the output-buffer voltage gain; A_dB is the same gain in decibels.

examples.question: An op-amp has input-stage gain Av1 = 100, gain-stage gain Av2 = 500, level-shifter gain Av3 = 0.5, and output-buffer gain Av4 = 0.98, all in V/V. Find the open-loop gain in V/V and in dB. For a differential input vid = 1 mV, find the ideal output and say whether a ±12 V supply clips it.
steps: Write the stage gains: Av1 = 100, Av2 = 500, Av3 = 0.5, Av4 = 0.98.
Input in volts: vid = 1 mV = 0.001 V.
Ideal output: Vout = A_ol × vid = 24,500 × 0.001 = 24.5 V.
The supply is ±12 V, so the largest possible magnitude is about 12 V, and less in practice. Since 24.5 V is greater than 12 V, the output clips.
examples.answer: The open-loop gain is 24,500 V/V, or 87.78 dB; a 1 mV input difference would demand 24.5 V, so on ±12 V supplies the output clips.
examples.check:
import math
Av1 = 100.0
Av2 = 500.0
Av3 = 0.5
Av4 = 0.98
A = Av1*Av2*Av3*Av4
AdB = 20*math.log10(A)
vid = 0.001
vout = A*vid
print(A)
print(round(AdB, 2))
print(vout)

traps: Multiplying stage gains in dB, or adding linear gains and calling the sum decibels. Convert each stage to dB and add, or multiply linear gains and convert once at the end.
Thinking the level shifter adds gain. It moves DC; its signal gain is at most about 1 and may be below 1, as Av3 = 0.5 shows.
Assuming the output can reach the supply rails. Saturation voltages and output-device drops keep the real swing below the rails.
Ignoring the output current limit. A heavy load or a short circuit can hit the limit, so the output voltage collapses even when the gain formula predicts a larger value.

quiz.q: Name the four internal functions of an op-amp in signal order.
quiz.a: Differential input stage, gain stage, level shifter, output buffer.

quiz.q: Why is the input stage built as a differential pair rather than a single amplifier?
quiz.a: It responds to the difference v_id and rejects the common-mode part, giving high CMRR. It also sets input resistance, input bias current, and offset.

quiz.q: An op-amp has Av1 = 80, Av2 = 400, Av3 = 0.6, and Av4 = 0.95. Find A_ol in V/V and in dB.
Why place a level shifter after the gain stage instead of using a resistor divider at the input?
quiz.a: The gain-stage output DC is too high for the output stage, so shifting there keeps the input signal unattenuated and preserves input resistance. A divider at the input would reduce the signal and load the source.

quiz.q: An op-amp has A_ol = 50,000 and vid = 0.5 mV on ±15 V supplies. Does the ideal output clip? Show the numbers.
quiz.a: Ideal Vout = 50,000 × 0.0005 = 25 V. The supply magnitude is 15 V, so 25 V is clipped; the real output stops below 15 V.

quiz.q: What sets CMRR in the input stage?
quiz.a: The tail current source output resistance and the matching of the differential pair and active load. Higher tail resistance and better matching raise CMRR.

quiz.q: What class is the output stage, and why is it used?
quiz.a: Class AB push-pull. It gives low crossover distortion and can source or sink load current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real op-amps use folded cascode and rail-to-rail input stages to get more gain and a wider input range on low supply voltages. Chopper and auto-zero techniques reduce offset for sensor signals. Current-feedback op-amps use a different topology for high slew rate. Search "folded cascode op-amp", "rail-to-rail input stage", and "chopper stabilized amplifier" to go further.
